etymologies.etymologyHTML: Recorded since 1297 as Middle English caucioun (“bail, guarantee, pledge”), from Old French caution (“security, surety”), itself from Latin cautiō, from cautus, past participle of caveō, cavēre (“be on one's guard”).

definitions.definition: Prudence when faced with, or when expecting to face, danger; care taken in order to avoid risk or harm.

quote.citation: c. 1599–1602 (date written), William Shakespeare, “The Tragedie of Hamlet, Prince of Denmarke”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act I, scene iii]:
quote.text: In way of caution I must tell you.

quote.citation: 1960 December, “Talking of Trains: The railways and the Devon floods”, in Trains Illustrated, page 709:
quote.text: [...] and on the Saturday heavy seas pounded the W.R. on its exposed coastal stretch between Dawlish and Teignmouth, loosening the ballast and forcing trains to proceed with extreme caution.

definitions.definition: A careful attention to the probable effects of an act, in order that failure or harm may be avoided.

quote.citation: 1702–1704, Edward [Hyde, 1st] Earl of Clarendon, “(please specify |book=I to XVI)”, in The History of the Rebellion and Civil Wars in England, Begun in the Year 1641. […], Oxford, Oxfordshire: Printed at the Theater, published 1707, →OCLC:
quote.text: The Parliament would yet give his majesty sufficient caution that the war should be vigorously prosecuted.

definitions.definition: (dated) One who draws attention or causes astonishment by their behaviour.

quote.citation: 1915, W. Somerset Maugham, Of Human Bondage, chapter 58:
quote.text: ‘You are a caution,’ she said, when she came out. ‘I don't understand you.’

definitions.definition: (law) A formal warning given as an alternative to prosecution in minor cases.
(transitive) To warn; to alert, advise that caution is warranted.
